output.brief: The enrolment drop is mainly a pricing effect, not an Admissions Office failure. Applications, admits and GPA all rose, so the applicant pool was not the problem. Yield fell by about the same amount for early-action admits (45.2% to 37.8%), whose decisions came out on time on the old system, as for regular-decision admits (39.0% to 31.5%), whose decisions were late. Slow turnaround therefore doesn't explain the fall. By scholarship tier, yield fell sharply only where award amounts were cut. Dean's yield went from 45.2% to 31.9% and Merit from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards were unchanged and yield stayed flat at about 36%. No-award yield also stayed roughly flat (38.5% to 37.0%). The Board's October 2025 schedule change relied on an old elasticity estimate. I'm fairly confident, though the tier data doesn't split early action from regular decision, and I didn't check the missing-transcript claims or the reader-staffing effect. Don't replace the director on this basis. Take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Also set a turnaround target for regular decision, since late answers are still a service problem. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the transcript issue is verified.
